headline: FDA still owes hemp cannabinoid lists before 12 November ban
dek: Congressional researchers say the FDA has published none of the lists or container guidance due on 10 February, days before the new hemp law starts.
key_points: On 12 November 2026, hemp products containing cannabinoids the plant cannot make naturally stop counting as hemp under federal law.
The FDA was ordered to publish lists of natural, THC-class and THC-like cannabinoids, plus guidance on the word 'container', by 10 February 2026.
A Congressional Research Service legal sidebar dated 28 October says none of those items has been published.
Most of the new hemp definition, including the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap, takes effect on 11 December 2026.
body: The first piece of the federal government's rewrite of hemp law takes effect on Thursday, 12 November 2026, and the agency Congress told to explain it has still not done so. The Food and Drug Administration was required to publish lists of cannabinoids and guidance on product containers by 10 February. Nine months later, none of it has appeared.

The gap was set out again in a Legal Sidebar from the Congressional Research Service, Congress's in-house legal and policy analysts, dated 28 October. It states plainly that the FDA had not published any of the required items as of that date. Marijuana Moment reported on 9 November that this is at least the third time CRS has flagged the missed deadline, and that the FDA had not answered its repeated requests for comment.

The new hemp definition came in a November 2025 spending law, Public Law 119-37, which CRS calls the Hemp Definition Amendment. It replaced the 2018 farm bill test, which looked only at delta-9 THC, with a total THC test of 0.3% on a dry-weight basis that also counts compounds such as delta-8, delta-10 and THC-O. It also carved several categories of product out of the definition of hemp altogether.

A second law passed in September 2026, Public Law 119-103, pushed most of those changes back to 11 December 2026. It left one exclusion on the original timetable. From 12 November, hemp-derived cannabinoid products that contain cannabinoids 'not capable of being naturally produced' by the cannabis plant are no longer hemp. CRS says such products will be treated as controlled substances to the extent they fall within the Controlled Substances Act's definitions of marijuana or THC.

The 11 December changes are broader. They exclude cannabinoids that the plant can make but that were synthesised or manufactured outside it, intermediate products above 0.3% total THC, and final consumer products holding more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC and similar cannabinoids per container. That cap is the provision that would remove most intoxicating hemp drinks, gummies and vapes from the legal market.

The 2025 law gave the FDA 90 days to publish four things: a list of all cannabinoids known to the agency that the cannabis plant can produce naturally; a list of the THC-class cannabinoids known to occur naturally in the plant; a list of other cannabinoids with effects similar to THC, or marketed as having them; and 'additional information and specificity' on the term container.

Each one matters for compliance. The first list is the dividing line for the 12 November exclusion: a seller needs to know whether a compound in its product is one the plant can make. The second and third lists define what counts toward the 0.4 milligram cap from 11 December. The container guidance decides how that cap is measured. The statute defines a container as the innermost packaging in direct contact with the product, such as a jar, bottle, packet, can or cartridge, but it does not settle every case, such as multi-serving packs.
> A ban that depends on a list nobody has published leaves compliance to guesswork, and leaves enforcement to whoever reads the gap most aggressively.
## Why the silence costs the industry

Hemp operators have warned for months that they cannot price inventory or reformulate products against definitions that do not exist. In August, Cornbread Hemp co-founder Jim Higdon told Marijuana Moment it was hard to comply while key definitions were still in question. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, the FDA's parent, told the outlet earlier this year that the agency intended to publish the lists on time in the Federal Register. It did not, and officials have not given a new date.

The uncertainty reaches beyond small shops. Village Farms said in its third-quarter results on 9 November that its Balanced Health Botanicals CBD unit is waiting for regulatory clarity on the 11 December change before deciding how to pursue a Medicare pilot for CBD products. States are not waiting either: as we reported on 9 November, Illinois sellers have sued to stop a state hemp law starting on 12 November, and South Carolina sellers are bracing for the federal date.

The 12 November exclusion is narrow on paper. It reaches cannabinoids that do not occur in the plant at all, a category CRS discusses at length because the law does not name them. Without the FDA's list, sellers of products built on converted or novel compounds must decide for themselves whether those compounds could be produced naturally. Getting that wrong would mean holding a controlled substance rather than a farm product. Retailers, distributors and payment processors are likely to take the cautious view and pull anything doubtful, regardless of how a court might later rule.

The larger shock is still a month away. Unless Congress acts again, 11 December brings the per-container THC cap and the end of most intoxicating hemp products as they are now sold. Lawmakers delayed the change once to allow time to write a regulatory framework instead; no such framework has passed.

Watch whether the FDA publishes anything before 12 November, and whether it arrives in the Federal Register as HHS promised. Watch for DEA or Justice Department statements on how they will treat products that lose hemp status, and for state attorneys general moving first, as Missouri's has against unlicensed sellers. Then watch Congress in the weeks before 11 December: the incoming Democratic majority does not take its seats until January, so any further delay or regulatory bill has to come from the current Congress.
